The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
User-facing copy changed (organiser -> organizer) in a refactor

The user-facing note text shown to attendees when calendar notes are hidden changed from "Notes have been hidden by the organiser" to "Notes have been hidden by the organizer". This wording change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar array refactor and is being slipped into a bug fix PR; the previous string was already shipped to end users and the rest of the codebase keeps "organise/organiser" spellings. A refactor like this should not change user-visible copy without an explicit reason.

deleteEvent deletes from 'primary' instead of the booking's destination calendar

Mirror of the updateEvent bug: the new fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` returns `undefined` whenever `externalCalendarId` is `null`/`undefined`, because the predicate becomes `cal.externalId === undefined` and never matches. `calendarId` therefore becomes `undefined`, and the existing `calendarId ? calendarId : defaultCalendarId` then makes `calendar.events.delete` target the user's "primary" calendar. The previous code returned the booking's destination calendar's externalId directly. As a result, cancel/delete flows on bookings whose reference has no `externalCalendarId` will now attempt to delete from the wrong Google calendar (and only succeed if the event happens to live in "primary", or silently 404 otherwise). This is reachable via `handleCancelBooking.ts` and `EventManager.updateAllCalendarEvents`'s old-event cleanup.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token"

When `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` is falsy, the code assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"` to the field and then saves it to the credential key in the DB. On the next token refresh the OAuth provider is sent `refresh_token="refresh_token"`, which it will reject (typically with `invalid_grant`), causing the credential to be marked invalid and the integration to break. The intent appears to have been to set a sentinel, but the value is being persisted and used as a real refresh token.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`minimumTokenResponseSchema` is malformed and rejects expected fields

The schema uses computed property names `[z.string().toString()]`. Both expressions evaluate to the same string representation of the ZodString instance (e.g. `"ZodString"`), so the object literal has two duplicate keys and JavaScript silently drops the first. The resulting schema is effectively `{ access_token: z.string(), "<schema name>": z.unknown().optional() }` and does not actually declare the intended catchall/number/expiry rules. Any non-`access_token` field (`expires_in`, `refresh_token`, `scope`, `expiry_date`, etc.) is stripped by ZodObject's default stripping behavior. With sharing enabled, every caller ends up with an `access_token` only, breaking the downstream code that depends on those fields (e.g. `googleCredentials.expiry_date`, `hubspotRefreshToken.expiresIn`, salesforce fields).

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Stores the full SafeParseResult instead of `.data`

`parseRefreshTokenResponse` returns the raw `SafeParseReturnType` object (`{ success, data }`). The Google Calendar code assigns this directly: `const key = parseRefreshTokenResponse(googleCredentials, googleCredentialSchema);` and then passes `key` to `prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`. The stored value will be `{ success: true, data: { ...googleCredentials } }` rather than the credentials object itself. On the next read, `googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key)` will fail because the top-level shape is wrong, marking the credential invalid. Other call sites (`office365calendar`, `salesforce`, `zoomvideo`) correctly use `.data`; this one does not.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent response shape breaks callers when sharing is enabled

When sharing is OFF, `refreshFunction` returns whatever the app's native refresh returns (a Google `GaxiosResponse` for googlecalendar, an Axios response for hubspot/zoho-bigin/zohocrm, a raw `fetch` `Response` for larkcalendar/office365calendar/office365video/webex/zoomvideo). When sharing is ON, the function instead returns a raw `fetch` `Response` from the sync endpoint. The code after the call expects the native shape — e.g. googlecalendar uses `res?.data`, hubspot uses `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken`/`expiresIn`, zoho-bigin/zohocrm use `tokenInfo.data.error` — which are absent on a `Response`. With sharing enabled, every one of these integrations will fail on token refresh (silently for hubspot because the result is just `undefined`; loudly for the rest because they try to read properties of `undefined`). The function should either return a normalized token object in both modes or document/enforce a single shape.

true_positives.golden_comment: When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent response shape breaks callers when sharing is enabled

When sharing is OFF, `refreshFunction` returns whatever the app's native refresh returns (a Google `GaxiosResponse` for googlecalendar, an Axios response for hubspot/zoho-bigin/zohocrm, a raw `fetch` `Response` for larkcalendar/office365calendar/office365video/webex/zoomvideo). When sharing is ON, the function instead returns a raw `fetch` `Response` from the sync endpoint. The code after the call expects the native shape — e.g. googlecalendar uses `res?.data`, hubspot uses `hubspotRefreshToken.accessToken`/`expiresIn`, zoho-bigin/zohocrm use `tokenInfo.data.error` — which are absent on a `Response`. With sharing enabled, every one of these integrations will fail on token refresh (silently for hubspot because the result is just `undefined`; loudly for the rest because they try to read properties of `undefined`). The function should either return a normalized token object in both modes or document/enforce a single shape.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Refresh triggers on any non-OK statusText, fragile to HTTP/2

`if (response.statusText !== "OK") throw new HttpError({ statusCode: 400, message: response.statusText })` relies on the HTTP/1.x statusText being exactly `"OK"`. Under HTTP/2 status reason phrases are not transmitted (and many proxies/clients return lowercase or empty), so a successful Salesforce response can throw here. Use `response.ok` (or `response.status >= 200 && response.status < 300`) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `jsforce.Connection` is created using stale `credentialKey.access_token` and `credentialKey.instance_url` after a token refresh, which can lead to authentication failures and incorrect data access. Ensure that the connection is established using the refreshed token values instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Manually refreshed Salesforce token is never given to the returned Connection

`getClient` performs a manual refresh, persists the new access token, and then constructs `new jsforce.Connection({ ..., accessToken: credentialKey.access_token, refreshToken: credentialKey.refresh_token })` using the OLD `credentialKey` values that were captured before the refresh. The freshly obtained `accessToken`/`instance_url` from the refresh response is written to the DB but never used by the jsforce client, so the Connection immediately operates with a stale token and jsforce will re-refresh on first use — duplicating and racing with the manual refresh.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Credential `appId` is taken from `appStoreMetadata` instead of the validated DB slug

The handler validates `reqBody.appSlug` against the `App` table but then looks the slug up in `appStoreMetadata` and stores `appId: appMetadata.slug`. If those two ever diverge, the credential row is keyed by a slug that doesn't exist in the `App` table, breaking downstream queries that join on `appId`. Use the validated `app.slug` for the stored `appId`.

Missing `prisma` import causes ReferenceError at runtime

The new refresh logic in `getClient` calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: ... } })`, but the file's import block (lines 1-20) does not import `prisma`. There is no `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. The function will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined` the first time `getClient` is invoked, breaking all Salesforce calendar/video operations in the new code path.

No replay protection, rate limit, or audit trail on credential upsert

Anyone holding the webhook secret can repeatedly overwrite or create credentials for any `userId` in the request body. There is no timestamp/nonce check to block replays, no per-IP rate limit, no per-user limit, and no record of which credentials were written or by whom. Combined with the timing-vulnerable comparison and the unencrypted `userId` in the body, a leak or brute-force of the secret lets an attacker plant OAuth tokens for arbitrary users. Consider adding a signed timestamp window, request signing, and structured logging of (userId, appSlug, request IP) for each upsert.

Outbound call to credential sync endpoint has no authentication

`fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` only sends `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the form body, with no shared secret, signature, or HMAC. Anyone able to reach this endpoint (or to observe/intercept traffic to it) can trigger token-refresh lookups for arbitrary users. At a minimum, send the same `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` (or a dedicated HMAC) as a header so the operator's app store can authenticate the caller.

Returns refreshed token even when the response carries an error

`if (!tokenInfo.data.error) { ... } else { this.log.error(tokenInfo.data); }` logs the error but then falls through to `return tokenInfo.data as BiginToken`. If the refresh response contains `{ error: "invalid_grant" }` (and `refreshOAuthTokens` returns the sync endpoint's raw `Response`, which lacks `.data.error`), the caller gets a fake/empty token and downstream calls fail opaquely. Reject on `error` or any non-2xx status instead of returning the payload.

Webhook header name is taken from env without normalization

`req.headers[process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME || "calcom-webhook-secret"]` uses the env var as an object key into `req.headers` directly. HTTP header lookup is normally case-insensitive and Node lowercases incoming headers; if the operator sets `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_HEADER_NAME` in mixed/upper case the lookup silently misses and the endpoint falls through to `403` for legitimate calls (or, if unset, hardcoded). Lowercase the value before use and validate it against `/^[a-z0-9-]+$/` so it cannot be used to probe internal headers or cause lookup confusion.

Webhook secret compared with `!==` (timing attack)

The header value is compared to `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` using `!==`, which short-circuits on the first mismatching byte and leaks timing information that can be used to brute-force the secret. Use a constant-time comparison such as `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over equal-length buffers (after a length check) instead. The endpoint is unauthenticated by any other mechanism (no rate limit, no IP allowlist, no replay protection), so the secret is the only barrier.

`APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` does not reflect the actual sync endpoint

The constant is defined as `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET && process.env.CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY`. Both `parseRefreshTokenResponse` and `refreshOAuthTokens` additionally require `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` to take the sharing branch. With only the first two variables set, the webhook will accept and store credentials but every token refresh silently falls back to the local OAuth path, which will not yield the shared token. Either include `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` in the constant or split it into two flags with clear semantics so operators see a consistent state.

findFirst + create/update race can produce duplicate credentials

The handler does `findFirst({ userId, appId })` then either `update` or `create` based on whether one was found. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same (userId, appSlug) can both find nothing and both `create`, producing duplicate `Credential` rows. The code's own comment notes that upsert can't be used because the credential id is unknown, but a `UNIQUE` constraint on `(userId, appId, type)` plus catching the unique-violation and falling back to update, or wrapping the find+create in a serializable transaction, would prevent duplicates that later cause inconsistent OAuth behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Email comparison for dedup and blacklist is case-sensitive

The dedup against existing attendees (`guest === attendee.email`) and the blacklist filter (`blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`) compare raw strings. Email local parts are conventionally treated as case-insensitive, so users can submit `User@Example.com` and bypass both checks even though `user@example.com` is already an attendee or blacklisted. All comparisons should lowercase both sides (the blacklist is already lowercased on parsing, but the input `guest` and the existing `attendee.email` are not).

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Permission check requires being both team admin AND team owner

`isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`, which means a regular team admin who is not also the team owner is rejected by the guard, and the request falls through to `isOrganizer`/`isAttendee`. For team bookings where the booking was assigned to another host, this incorrectly denies legitimate team admins from adding guests. The two role checks should be combined with `||` (or just call `isTeamAdmin`, which typically implies owner privileges) so team admins are allowed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Emails are computed from the original `guests` list instead of the deduplicated one

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the raw input, but the DB write only used `uniqueGuests` (deduped against existing attendees and the blacklist). In `email-manager.ts`, attendees whose email appears in `newGuests` receive a fresh `AttendeeScheduledEmail`; this causes any email that was filtered out only as a duplicate of an existing attendee (e.g. an attendee resubmits their own email) to receive a duplicate booking-confirmation email as if they were just added. Pass `uniqueGuests` so the notification logic mirrors what was actually persisted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Initial state is `[""]` so the form starts in an invalid state

`useState<string[]>([""])` seeds the input with one empty email; pressing 'Add' immediately triggers `ZAddGuestsInputSchema.safeParse`, which fails on `z.string().email()` against `""`, surfacing the red 'emails must be unique and valid' banner before the user has typed anything. Initialize with `[]` (matching the empty-state branch of `MultiEmail`) or run validation only after the first onChange.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar update runs with the caller's credentials, not the organizer's

`EventManager` is constructed with `...user` and `credentials` obtained via `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` (the logged-in user). When the caller is a team admin or an attendee (both of whom the permission check above allows), they typically don't have the host's calendar integration, so `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` either fails outright or attempts the update under the wrong account. The organizer of the booking is already fetched at line 58; the manager should be built from that user's id/credentials so the calendar invite is actually pushed to the new guests.

Client-side validation reports generic 'unique and valid' even when emails clash with existing attendees

`ZAddGuestsInputSchema` only checks email syntax and mutual uniqueness of the typed list. It does not know about attendees already on the booking, so when the user types an email that is already a guest, the request is still sent and the server responds with `emails_must_be_unique_valid`, which the dialog surfaces verbatim even though the values were unique within the user's input. Either pre-filter the input against the booking's existing attendee emails in the dialog (the booking is already known at render time) or pick a more specific translation key on the server when the dedup against `booking.attendees` is what failed.

Component mutates the `value` prop

`value = value || []` reassigns the incoming prop before reading it. React props must be treated as immutable; this both violates React conventions and breaks if a parent passes a value of `null` vs `undefined` differently. Default-clone to a local `const` instead, e.g. `const values = value ?? [];`.

DB write is committed before calendar update with no transaction

`prisma.booking.update(...)` (line 92) creates the attendee rows first, then `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` is called separately, and only afterwards are the notification emails sent. If the calendar sync throws (e.g. bad credentials, see line 158) or the email send throws, the booking already has the new attendees persisted but no calendar invite went out; the client receives an error and the user is left in an inconsistent state where the API claims failure but guests are in the DB. Wrap the DB write and the external calls in a compensating/transactional pattern, or perform the calendar update first (with idempotency) and only persist attendees on success.

Email-send errors are silently swallowed

`sendAddGuestsEmails` is wrapped in `try { ... } catch (err) { console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails"); }`. The project uses a structured logger elsewhere (`logger` is already imported in this file); a plain `console.log` drops context, and swallowing the error means neither the caller nor an operator will notice that attendees were added but never notified. At minimum this should log via the project's `logger` (with `safeStringify` of the error) and ideally surface a non-fatal warning in the response.

Error toast prefixes the TRPC error code in front of the translated message

On mutation error the toast is built as `${err.data?.code}: ${t(err.message)}`. Error codes like `BAD_REQUEST`, `FORBIDDEN`, `NOT_FOUND` are leaked to end users alongside the translated message (e.g. 'BAD_REQUEST: Emails must be unique and valid'). Codes are an internal contract; show only `t(err.message)`, falling back to `t("unable_to_add_guests")` when the key is missing or untranslatable.

New tRPC mutation ships without tests

The PR adds a non-trivial mutation with a permission check, blacklist filtering, calendar sync, and email fan-out, but no test file is included. At least the following cases need coverage before merge: (1) team admin OR team owner is allowed, plain team member who is not the host is rejected; (2) emails matching an existing attendee (case-insensitively) are filtered out; (3) blacklisted emails are filtered out; (4) calendar failure does not leave the booking partially updated; (5) the new guests receive the guest-added email rather than a duplicate booking confirmation.

Newly added guests receive a generic booking confirmation, not a guest-added notice

For attendees that match `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`, the manager instantiates `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (the base class), whose subject/content is the standard 'Your booking is confirmed' wording. Existing attendees get `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` with subject `guests_added_event_type_subject`. The newly invited guest therefore sees a confirmation email phrased as if they had booked the event themselves, with no hint that they were added by someone else. Either reuse `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail` (it already generates a `REQUEST` ICS method) or pass the `guests_added_event_type_subject`/`new_guests_added` keys down so the message matches the situation.

Schema imposes no length bounds on the `guests` array

`ZAddGuestsInputSchema` accepts `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `min`/`max`. A direct API caller can submit an arbitrarily large list (or an empty list that the handler then rejects with a generic error), enabling trivial abuse and unbounded cost from calendar/email fan-out on the server. Add a reasonable `.min(1).max(N)` (the existing dialog caps UI input to a small number) so the endpoint cannot be weaponised through a single request.

replyTo header exposes every attendee's email address

`replyTo: [this.calEvent.organizer.email, ...this.calEvent.attendees.map(({ email }) => email)]` puts every attendee into the `Reply-To` header. Mail clients honor `Reply-To` and will deliver the response to every address listed there, so when the organizer (or any recipient) hits Reply, the message is broadcast to all attendees. The base `OrganizerScheduledEmail` only uses the organizer's email in `replyTo`; this template should do the same. Otherwise the organizer is one click away from leaking a private reply to the entire guest list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount-based deleteMany is not scoped to SMS method

The new OR branch `retryCount: { gt: 1 }` in the cleanup deleteMany does not filter by `method`. The original deleteMany was intentionally restricted to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` because the SMS scheduling cron is the only owner of those rows; EMAIL/WHATSAPP reminders have their own cron paths. With this change, ANY WorkflowReminder row with retryCount > 1 will be deleted by this SMS handler, regardless of method. Today only this file increments retryCount, so there is no immediate data loss, but the cleanup now silently reaches across reminder types and will cause unexpected deletions the moment retryCount is reused for EMAIL or WHATSAPP elsewhere. Scope the clause to `{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 } }`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
Catch block increments retryCount after Twilio already accepted the SMS

The try block can throw from the success-path `prisma.workflowReminder.update({ scheduled: true, referenceId: scheduledSMS.sid })` (lines 169-177) AFTER `twilio.scheduleSMS` has already returned a truthy result and Twilio has accepted the message. The catch handler then unconditionally increments retryCount. Consequence: retryCount grows on a row whose Twilio message is already scheduled, and because `scheduled` is still false in the DB the next cron run will call `twilio.scheduleSMS` again, producing a duplicate SMS to the user. The retryCount bump must only happen when the Twilio call itself failed (or returned falsy), not when the bookkeeping update of an already-scheduled reminder fails.

No tests added for the new retryCount behaviour

The PR changes observable behaviour (WorkflowReminder rows are now deleted after 2 failed schedule attempts, and the new retryCount column drives that decision), but ships no unit or integration tests. At minimum the following cases should be covered: (1) twilio.scheduleSMS returns falsy -> retryCount incremented to 1, row preserved; (2) two consecutive falsy returns -> row deleted by the next cron run; (3) twilio.scheduleSMS throws -> retryCount incremented via the catch path; (4) twilio.scheduleSMS throws AND subsequent update throws -> loop continues for the remaining reminders. Without these the retry semantics can silently regress.

Scheduling failures logged via console.log instead of console.error

The catch handler at line 198 logs the error with `console.log`, so in production this surfaces at the same severity as the routine info logs. Should be `console.error` so the failure is captured by the standard error pipeline (and the message includes the booking/reminder id, not just the raw error object).

Unhandled throw from catch-block update aborts the rest of the cron batch

The catch block performs a `prisma.workflowReminder.update` that is not itself wrapped in a try/catch. If that update fails (e.g. the row was concurrently deleted by another worker, or a transient DB error) the exception escapes the for-loop and the request returns 500 before processing the remaining reminders in `unscheduledReminders`. Wrap the catch-block update in its own try/catch (or log-and-continue) so one failed update cannot skip the rest of the batch.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Caching describe block removed; coverage lost for cachedAuthConditions and cachedFilterConditions

The "Caching" describe block (which previously contained `should cache authorization conditions` and `should cache filter conditions` tests that asserted the second call returned an object structurally equal to the first) has been deleted from the test file. This drops all coverage for the `cachedAuthConditions` and `cachedFilterConditions` memoization in `getAuthorizationConditions` and `getFilterConditions`. If caching regresses (e.g., conditions are rebuilt on every call, causing an extra DB roundtrip per request, or a future change forgets to invalidate the cache when options/filters change), no test will detect it. The deleted block was located where the new `describe("getBaseConditions", ...)` (line 437) now begins.

Integration test relies on BookingTimeStatusDenormalized being populated synchronously by triggers

The "should combine authorization and filter conditions" test creates a booking directly via `prisma.booking.create(...)` and then queries `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` with `prisma.$queryRaw`, expecting exactly `[{ id: userBooking.id }]`. `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` is a denormalized table that is normally populated by PostgreSQL triggers on Booking INSERTs/UPDATEs. If those triggers are absent in the test environment, are disabled, or run asynchronously, the booking will not appear in the denormalized table and the assertion will fail with an empty array. The PR author explicitly acknowledges they could not run the integration tests due to test-runner configuration issues and asks the reviewer to verify execution manually; this specific test is the most fragile in the suite and the most likely to fail.

findMany method removed from public API; callers will break at runtime

The `findMany(findManyArgs: Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedFindManyArgs)` method has been removed and replaced with `getBaseConditions(): Promise<Prisma.Sql>`. This is a breaking change to the public API of `InsightsBookingService`. Any callers in the codebase (e.g., routing layers, controller handlers, or other services) that invoke `service.findMany(...)` will fail at runtime with `TypeError: service.findMany is not a function`. The PR description frames this as a test-update PR, but the diff also rewrites the service. No callers of `findMany` are updated in this diff; if any exist they must be migrated to obtain the SQL fragment via `getBaseConditions()` and execute it with `prisma.$queryRaw` (or similar).

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data – no-op

The new call `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {});` passes an empty object as `data`. Prisma's `updateMany` only updates fields explicitly listed in `data`, so with `{}` no columns (including the Prisma-managed `updatedAt`) are touched. The preceding comment "Update SelectedCalendar.updatedAt for all calendars under this credential" is therefore wrong – the call is a silent no-op. Either pass `updatedAt: new Date()` (or similar) to actually achieve the documented effect, or remove the call entirely. Note also that the PR description indicates `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is only updated by the webhook handler and is not displayed in the UI, so this added line is likely dead code that obscures the actual cache-refresh flow.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
macOS-only sed in-place edit breaks on Linux

Line 68 uses `sed -i '' -E ...`. The `''` after `-i` is BSD/macOS syntax (sed takes a mandatory backup-suffix argument, with empty meaning no backup). On GNU sed (Linux/CI containers), `-i` does not take an argument and the script becomes `sed: invalid option -- 'E'` / treats `''` as the script. The PR's CI runs on Linux, so the script will fail on a fresh checkout. Use `sed -i.bak` followed by `rm *.bak`, or branch on the platform (e.g., `[[ "$OSTYPE" == darwin* ]] && SED_INPLACE="sed -i ''" || SED_INPLACE="sed -i"`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Authorization failure throws generic Error – not a TRPCError

When the credential isn't owned by the caller, the handler throws a plain `new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. This surfaces as an opaque `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` over tRPC, gives the client the same status as a true server bug, and merges the two failure modes (not-found vs forbidden) into one message. Use `throw new TRPCError({ code: "FORBIDDEN", message: "Credential not found or access denied" })` (or `NOT_FOUND` after a `findUnique`). That also makes the existing "Error deleting cache" toast in `CredentialActionsDropdown` distinguishable from genuine infrastructure failures if more granular handling is added later.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
DropdownItem nested inside DropdownMenuItem produces invalid nested-button markup

Both "Delete cached data" and "Remove App" actions are written as `<DropdownMenuItem><DropdownItem .../></DropdownMenuItem>`. Since `DropdownMenuItem` (Radix) is itself an interactive `<button>`/menuitem, and `DropdownItem` is a styled `<button>` from the same dropdown module, the rendered DOM becomes a button-in-button (invalid HTML, screen-reader/AT issues) and creates competing onClick handlers with confusing focus/hover states. Typically cal.com uses either DropdownMenuItem with text, OR DropdownItem (without the wrapping DropdownMenuItem) for styled actions. Remove the wrapping `DropdownMenuItem` around `DropdownItem` (or replace DropdownItem with plain text/icon inside the item) so that exactly one button is rendered per row.

New deleteCache tRPC mutation and handler have no tests

This PR adds a brand-new destructive tRPC route (`viewer.calendars.deleteCache`) along with its handler, plus two new repository methods (`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds`, `updateManyByCredentialId`) and a new UI component (`CredentialActionsDropdown`). None of these have accompanying unit/integration tests. The handler in particular performs authorization (verifying the credential belongs to the calling user) and a destructive DB op (`calendarCache.deleteMany`), and is exactly the kind of cross-cutting call most worth covering. Please add tests for: (a) another user cannot delete your cache (authorization), (b) missing/invalid credentialId is rejected by zod, (c) `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` excludes expired entries (after the fix above) and groups multiple cache rows per credential correctly, and (d) `CredentialActionsDropdown` calls `connectedCalendars.invalidate` after a successful delete (after the fix above).

Stale generated warning comment contradicts the migration body

Prisma's autogenerated warning still claims: "Added the required column `updatedAt` to the `CalendarCache` table without a default value. This is not possible if the table is not empty." The actual SQL adds `DEFAULT NOW()`, so the table *is* populated safely for existing rows. Leaving the contradictory header in place is confusing for future migrations/maintenance and for anyone reading the migration file. Either drop the Prisma warning block (since the developer manually fixed it) or replace it with a short comment explaining why a `DEFAULT NOW()` was used instead of `@updatedAt` for legacy rows.

deleteCache mutation does not invalidate connectedCalendars – stale cache status remains in UI

`deleteCacheMutation` only fires a toast and the optional `onSuccess?.()` callback. Unlike `disconnectMutation` further down (which invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` and `viewer.apps.integrations` in `onSettled`), `deleteCacheMutation` does not call `utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars.invalidate()`. The platform-atom wrapper passes `onChanged` as the `onSuccess`, which is a consumer-defined callback that is not guaranteed to refetch the tRPC query. After a successful cache deletion the user will continue to see the previous "Last updated: <timestamp>" under "Cache Status" until a full page reload, even though the underlying rows are gone. Add an `onSettled` (or `onSuccess`) that invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` to match the disconnect flow.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt – reports status for expired cache rows

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` runs `groupBy` over `CalendarCache` with no `expiresAt` filter, so a credential whose only cache rows are past `expiresAt` still returns a row and the UI then renders a "Last updated: <old timestamp>" plus a "Delete cached data" entry. In contrast, `getCachedAvailability` correctly filters `expiresAt: { gte: new Date() }`, so the user is told the cache exists/is recent even though no actual cache hit will ever occur. Add an `expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) }` clause (or filter post-groupBy) so the displayed "Last updated" matches what `getCachedAvailability` would consider usable.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fire-and-forget pattern in workflow reminder cancellations across the codebase

The workflow-reminder cancellation code uses `forEach` whose async callbacks are not awaited, so the cancellation calls run in the background while the caller continues and returns its HTTP response. Affected locations: `handleCancelBooking.ts:485-493`, `handleNewBooking.ts:967-973`, `bookings.tsx:488-494`, and `workflows.tsx:212-218, 376-382, 519-525, 574-580`. In serverless deployments the function instance can be frozen right after the response is returned, which may abort in-flight SendGrid/Twilio cancellation requests. Errors from these calls are also silently swallowed; for example, the `try/catch` in `handleNewBooking.ts:965-976` cannot catch anything from an unawaited `forEach` and the error log inside `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` is the only signal. These loops should use `Promise.all(items.map(...))` so cancellations and errors are observed before the response is sent. In `workflows.tsx:212-218` the forEach is followed immediately by `workflow.deleteMany`, so the cascade can delete the reminder rows before the SendGrid/Twilio requests even fire, making the cancellations effectively lost.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteScheduledEmailReminder with immediateDelete=true silently swallows SendGrid errors without a DB fallback

When `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` is called with `immediateDelete=true` (used by `handleNewBooking.ts:969` for rescheduling and `workflows.tsx:214, 521` for workflow/step deletion), it sends a cancel request to SendGrid and returns. If that request fails (e.g., because the 100 pending-cancellation quota mentioned in the PR description is reached), the catch block at line 233 only logs the error and the function returns without writing anything to the database. The new CRON in `scheduleEmailReminders.ts:44-51` only selects reminders where `cancelled: true`, so the failed cancellation is never retried and SendGrid will still send the email. The function should set `cancelled: true` (or otherwise record that the DB row needs CRON handling) regardless of SendGrid success so the CRON can retry the cancellation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
CRON query for cancelled reminders is missing the method filter

The `remindersToCancel` query at lines 44-51 selects `WorkflowReminder` rows with `cancelled: true` and `scheduledDate <= now+1h`. It does not include `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL`. Today only `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` sets `cancelled: true`, so in practice the rows are email rows, but the missing filter is fragile: if a future change (or a bad data fix) ever sets the flag on an SMS row, the CRON will call `client.request` against `/v3/user/scheduled_sends` with a Twilio SID as the `batch_id`, sending SendGrid a request it cannot honor and producing a misleading error in the catch block at line 75. Add `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` to the `where` clause.

No tests added for the new workflow-reminder cancellation logic

The PR makes several non-trivial changes to a flow that previously had a production bug (#7225): a new nullable `cancelled` field on `WorkflowReminder`, a deferred SendGrid cancellation performed by the `scheduleEmailReminders` CRON inside a 1-hour window, a new `immediateDelete` branch in `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`, and new cancellation paths added to `handleNewBooking.ts`, `handleCancelBooking.ts`, `bookings.tsx`, and `workflows.tsx`. No unit or integration tests were added to verify any of: (1) cancelling a booking actually prevents a previously scheduled workflow email from being delivered, (2) rescheduling cancels old reminders and schedules new ones without duplicates, (3) the CRON handles reminders inside and outside the 1-hour window correctly, (4) the SendGrid quota failure path falls back to the CRON, (5) workflow/step deletion truly stops email delivery for the removed workflow. For a fix to a reported production bug this leaves the regression risk unaddressed.

Sequential SendGrid cancellation requests in the CRON

The `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop at lines 56-74 awaits each SendGrid `client.request` call one after another, then collects the corresponding prisma deletes. When many cancelled reminders have accumulated (e.g., after a bulk cancellation or a long CRON outage), this serial processing stretches the CRON run time and may exceed its execution budget. The SendGrid requests should be parallelised with `Promise.all(remindersToCancel.map(...))`; the prisma deletes can still be awaited together afterward.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async ...) fires calendar/video deletions without awaiting

The block `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not wait for the async callback. `Array.prototype.forEach` ignores returned promises, so every `getCalendar(...)` and `calendar.deleteEvent(...)` / `deleteMeeting(...)` call is fire-and-forget. The surrounding `try/catch` cannot catch rejections from awaited code either, so any failure becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Consequence: the surrounding `Reschedule` function continues to `await director.buildForRescheduleEmail()`, then `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)`, then returns `true` before the calendar/video deletions actually happen (or they may never finish if the request is short-lived). Bookings are reported as rescheduled while the previous calendar events and video rooms remain on the user's calendar. Fix: replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
No handling when dynamic import resolves to undefined

After the change, `appStore[calendarType.split("_").join("") as keyof typeof appStore]` returns `Promise<... | undefined>` for unknown keys. `await` on the resulting `undefined` yields `undefined`, so `calendarApp` becomes `undefined` and falls through to the `log.warn(...)` branch. That is fine, but the type assertion `as keyof typeof appStore` lies to TypeScript: the union of awaited values is not narrowed, so the `"lib" in calendarApp` guard works at runtime but the inferred type of `calendarApp` is `Promise<typeof import("applecalendar")> | Promise<typeof import("caldavcalendar")> | ... | undefined`, and `await` does not narrow the union the way the author likely intends. There is no runtime regression here, but the type cast masks a real value coming back as `undefined` for unknown calendar types and a missing `default` / explicit 404 path. Consider an explicit `if (!app) { log.warn(...); return null; }` before the `"lib" in app` check and remove the misleading `as keyof typeof appStore` cast.

Recurring event calendar deletions are not awaited

Inside the recurring-events branch the code does `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent); })`. `forEach` does not await async functions, so the iteration kicks off the work and returns. By the time the function reaches `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))`, the array is usually empty (or only partially populated), so the `Promise.all` resolves immediately and the response is sent. The actual calendar deletions run later (or not at all if the request lifecycle ends). For a paid/seated booking this means previously scheduled events can stay on the organizer's calendar after cancellation. Replace with `for (const credential of ...) { ... await ... apiDeletes.push(...); }` (as was done correctly in the non-recurring branch immediately below) or `await Promise.all(...)`.

forEach(async ...) fires calendar/video deletions without awaiting

Identical pattern to packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` does not await the async callbacks, so the calendar and video deletions start but are never waited on. The `try/catch` around the forEach only catches synchronous throws; awaited errors become unhandled rejections. The function then proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and returns `true`, so the caller is told the reschedule succeeded before (or even without) the previous calendar event being deleted. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`.

getCalendarCredentials is sync but now returns Promises in its objects

`getCalendarCredentials` keeps its synchronous signature but inside it now assigns `const calendar = getCalendar(credential);` (which became async). Every returned `{ integration, credential, calendar }` object therefore has `calendar: Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` was updated to `await item.calendar`; any other internal or external caller of `getCalendarCredentials` that still treats `item.calendar` as a synchronous value (or whose TS type comes from `ReturnType<typeof getCalendarCredentials>`) will silently break. Either make the function `async` (and `await getCalendar(...)` inside, then re-shape the return type) or change the field name (e.g. `calendarPromise`) so callers cannot accidentally use it unsynchronized.

requestReschedule returns before calendar/video deletions complete

Inside the `requestReschedule` mutation: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... })` runs all calendar/video deletions in parallel but does not await them. The mutation then proceeds to `await sendRequestRescheduleEmail(...)` and returns. Because `forEach` ignores returned promises and the awaited `getCalendar(...)`/`deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` calls happen asynchronously, the previous calendar events may not be removed before the reschedule email is sent and the mutation returns. Errors thrown inside the async callback become unhandled promise rejections because the surrounding `try/catch` (if any) is synchronous. Fix with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Copy-paste bug: `end` is identical to `start`

Inside the working-hours branch: `const start = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute(); const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`. Both expressions compute the slot's start minute-of-day, so the check degenerates to `start < workingHour.startTime || start > workingHour.endTime`. The slot's end time is never considered, so any booking that crosses the end of the working window (e.g. a 60-min event ending at 18:01) is silently treated as still inside the window. Almost certainly the intent was `end = slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
dayjs objects compared with === (always false)

The new code compares dayjs wrapper objects with `===`: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")`. Two distinct dayjs instances are never reference-equal even when they represent the same instant, so this branch never executes. This breaks the intended "override start === end means blocked all day" semantics and any other code that relies on this comparison. Use `.isSame()` or compare `.valueOf()` instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override test only covers whole-hour boundaries in a single day window

The new test asserts identical UTC slot times for the IST and Dhaka scenarios, but only for one whole-hour override (`14:00–18:00` IST). It does not exercise: overrides with non-zero minute components (e.g. 14:30), overrides that span midnight in either tz, half-hour offsets applied to *the override itself* rather than the invitee, DST transitions around the override day, or multiple overlapping overrides. The bug at `slots.ts:114` (`===` on dayjs objects) and the timezone-arithmetic in `packages/lib/slots.ts` are both invisible to the current matrix.

First half of the PR fix (round-robin with fixed-host date overrides) is not covered by any test

The PR description explicitly says it fixes two bugs: (1) date overrides of fixed hosts being ignored in round-robin events, and (2) date overrides not adjusting to invitee timezones. The only added test (`scheduleForEventOnADayWithDateOverrideDifferentTimezone`) covers (2) by re-running the existing single-user scenario with a different invitee tz. There is no scenario with `schedulingType: "ROUND_ROBIN"`, a fixed host with a date override, and a non-fixed host, asserting that the slot is suppressed on the override day. Without this, the round-robin-fixed-host behaviour change is unprotected against future regressions.

Local type for `dateOverrides` is narrower than the data actually passed in

The `dateOverrides` parameter is typed as `{ start: Date; end: Date; }[]`, but the callers spread `...schedule` where `schedule.dateOverrides` comes from `getUserAvailability` and contains extra fields (`userId`, and now `timeZone` from the type change). The narrowing is benign at runtime (extra fields are ignored), but it diverges from the `TimeRange` definition and will mislead future readers.

Missing null guard for `override.timeZone` will crash if undefined

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` is called unconditionally, but `override.timeZone` was just added as an *optional* field on `TimeRange` (`packages/types/schedule.d.ts`). `dayjs#tz` throws on `undefined`. The corresponding call inside `checkIfIsAvailable` (`trpc/.../slots.ts:107`) defensively uses `organizerTimeZone ? ... : 0`, but `packages/lib/slots.ts` does not. Any caller (current or future) that supplies a `DateOverride` without populating `timeZone` will crash slot generation. Either default `override.timeZone` to the schedule/user tz or guard the call.

Override day match depends on the host machine's local timezone

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes").format("YYYY MM DD")` builds a dayjs in the system default timezone and formats it without setting `.tz(organizerTimeZone)`, while the right-hand side `slotStartTime.format("YYYY MM DD")` is in UTC. The numeric offset shift is correct, but the format is then interpreted in whatever the server's local tz is, so the same override can match different days depending on whether the Node process is running in UTC, IST, etc. Production servers are rarely in UTC, so this introduces a flaky/cross-environment correctness bug that the test (which only runs the suite locally) cannot catch. Use `.tz(organizerTimeZone)` explicitly, or compare the day in a fixed reference (e.g. compare UTC day strings on both sides).

Stale/incorrect comments around the new date-override block

The comment `// slot is not within the date override` is placed above the `return false`, but `find` returning truthy here only means *at least one* override on the day didn't cover the slot — not that no override did. Likewise the trailing comment `//if no date override for slot exists check if it is within normal work hours` describes the working-hours branch, but the working-hours branch is also reached when `dateOverrideExist` is true and the slot is *inside* the override (i.e. always-true path). The comments do not match the control flow and will confuse future readers.

Working-hours comparison mixes UTC with organizer's timezone

`slotStartTime = time.utc()`, so `slotStartTime.hour()`/`.minute()`/`.day()` return UTC values, but `workingHour.startTime`/`endTime`/`days` are documented as "minutes since midnight; serialized to UTC by using the organizer timeZone" (i.e. expressed in the organizer's local timezone). The new check at line 143 (`start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime`) compares UTC minutes-of-day to organizer-TZ minutes-of-day, so for any non-UTC organizer the comparison is offset by the organizer's UTC offset. Concretely, an IST organizer with hours 9:30–18:00 IST and a slot at 14:00 IST (= 08:30 UTC) yields `start = 510` vs `workingHour.startTime = 570` and the slot is incorrectly flagged as outside working hours. This is not caught by the new test because that test's slots all happen to be covered by a date override, which short-circuits before the working-hours check.

`find` short-circuits across multiple overrides, can wrongly mark a covered slot unavailable

`dateOverrides.find(...)` returns truthy as soon as *any* override for the day is encountered that does not contain the slot. If the same day has two overrides and the slot is inside override A but outside override B, the iteration visits B, returns true, and the whole function returns `false` — even though the slot is legitimately covered by A. Either iterate all overrides first, set `dateOverrideExist` only when the slot is actually inside an override, and base the final return on whether the slot is inside *any* override (or whether *all* overrides exclude it, depending on intended semantics).

AssignmentSource.queued default evaluated at class-definition time, not per-instance

In a dataclass, the expression on the right-hand side of a field with a default value is evaluated once at class definition, not each time the dataclass is instantiated. true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() breaks out of loop on deadline, leaving later processes unterminated

In `SpanFlusher.join`, the iteration `for process_index, process in self.processes.items():` calls `break` as soon as the supplied `timeout` is exhausted. Any processes whose entries come after the one currently being inspected are never visited and never `terminate()`d. With N flusher processes and a short join deadline, the surviving subprocesses keep running after the consumer has been declared shut down; their Kafka producers and Redis state are not cleanly closed, which can leave pending produces (`producer_futures`) unresolved and produce duplicate or partial segments on the buffered-segments topic if the broker accepts the late flush. The loop must iterate over every process and just skip the wait portion (but still call `process.terminate()`) when the deadline has passed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

false_positives.candidate:
Any single flusher process hitting backpressure halts the entire consumer

In `submit`, the backpressure check raises `MessageRejected` if **any** of `self.process_backpressure_since.values()` is non-zero past the threshold. Because shards are partitioned round-robin across processes, a single problematic shard (or hot key on one shard) can stall the whole consumer even when other processes are healthy and keeping up. The pre-refactor behavior only had a single flusher, so this regression doesn't surface there. Consider aggregating backpressure over the whole pool (e.g. require a majority of processes to be in backpressure, or check that `drift` has grown large) so a straggler doesn't take down throughput.

Backpressure metric lost the shard/process dimension

Pre-refactor, the backpressure metric was emitted via `metrics.incr("spans.buffer.flusher.backpressure")` from a single flusher. After the refactor, the same metric is emitted from inside a loop over `self.process_backpressure_since.values()`, but no `tags` are attached. There is now no way to tell from metrics which flusher process (or shard group) is causing the consumer to be paused. The other flusher metrics in the file (e.g. `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy`, `spans.buffer.flusher.produce`) are correctly tagged with `{shard|shards}`. The backpressure metric should be tagged similarly, e.g. `tags={"process_index": process_index}` or `{"shards": shard_tag}`, so operators can attribute stalls.

Dead helper `_create_process_for_shard` is never invoked

The method `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is defined (lines 127–132) but is not called from anywhere in the module or tests. It will be flagged by static analyzers as unused and is leftover scaffolding. (Not a runtime bug, but a maintainer should remove it before merging.)

Docstring claims one process per shard, but implementation caps processes

The class docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but `__init__` actually creates `min(max_processes, len(buffer.assigned_shards))` processes and shards are shared across processes via round-robin when `max_processes < len(shards)`. This is misleading and contradicts both the new `--flusher-processes` CLI option (which defaults to 1) and the test `test_flusher_processes_limit` that exercises sharing. The docstring should describe the actual pooling behavior.

Per-process SpansBuffer in subprocesses can race with main-process writes

`_create_process_for_shards` constructs a brand-new `SpansBuffer(shards)` (`shard_buffer = SpansBuffer(shards)`) and pickles it into the spawned subprocess. The main consumer thread, however, was given a separate `SpansBuffer(assigned_shards=[p.index for p in partitions])` in `factory.py` and writes incoming spans via `buffer.process_spans(...)` on that object. Although both buffers are stateless wrappers over Redis, each subprocess now opens its own Redis connection pool from a different PID, and the flush logic does `buffer.flush_segments(now=now)` / `buffer.record_stored_segments()` against its private buffer. Nothing in the diff confirms this design is safe (e.g. that keys TTLs are observed the same way, or that `any_shard_at_limit`/`get_memory_info` look at the correct Redis instances consistently). The single-process version relied on one shared buffer; the refactor should validate or call out this assumption explicitly so a future change to `SpansBuffer` doesn't quietly break cross-process semantics.

Restarted process is killed but never joined, leaking zombies

In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a flusher process is unhealthy the code calls `process.kill()` and then immediately calls `self._create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` to spawn a replacement. The killed process is never `join()`ed and never `close()`d. With `MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS = 10` and any reasonable churn (e.g. SIGKILL exit codes, transient Redis issues during deployment), up to 10 `spawn`-context children can be left as zombies holding PIDs and OS resources until the parent exits. Repeated restarts during the consumer's lifetime will gradually leak OS resources. The fix is to `process.join(timeout=...)` (and ideally `process.close()`) after `kill()` before reassigning `self.processes[process_index]`.

`flusher_processes` declared `int | None` but only ever set to a CLI int

`ProcessSpansStrategyFactory.__init__` declares `flusher_processes: int | None = None` and `SpanFlusher.__init__` declares `max_processes: int | None = None`. Both fall back to `len(buffer.assigned_shards)` via `max_processes or len(...)`, where `or` would also coerce `0` to the fallback. If an operator ever passes `--flusher-processes 0` (deliberately to disable flushers, or via a config that defaults to 0), `0 or len(shards)` evaluates to `len(shards)`, silently spawning processes anyway. Either change `or` to a strict `is None` check or document that 0 is not a valid value.

test_flusher_processes_limit does not verify shard partitioning or end-to-end flushing

The new test only asserts `len(flusher.processes) == 2`, `flusher.max_processes == 2`, `flusher.num_processes == 2`, and that the shards total 4. It does not verify that (a) each shard is assigned to exactly one process (no duplicates / no missing shards), (b) the round-robin ordering is stable, (c) when `flusher_processes > len(assigned_shards)` the pool is capped, or (d) that spans sent to the consumer are actually flushed and emitted via `produce_to_pipe` for each process group. Without (d), a regression where one of the new per-process flushers silently stops emitting would not be caught. Without (a), a bug where every shard is assigned to `process_index=0` would still pass.

Inside `test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling`, two messages are submitted (offsets 100 and 101) and the first is configured to raise. The OrderedQueueWorker catches the exception, logs it, and still calls `complete_offset` for both, so the commit loop will commit offset 101 (last processed). However the test ends with `assert len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, which asserts that NO commits happen for the partition. This contradicts the docstring ("errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages") and means the test passes whether or not the desired behavior is implemented. The assertion should be the opposite, e.g. `assert test_partition in committed_offsets` and `assert committed_offsets[test_partition] == 102` (101 + 1, mirroring the +1 in `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker.commit_offsets`).

false_positives.candidate:
--mode help text still describes only 'parallel uses multithreading'

The `uptime_options()` click choices were extended to include `thread-queue-parallel` but the help string still reads `"The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading."`. Operators picking a mode from `--help` have no indication that the new option exists or what it does. Either update the help text to enumerate the modes (and describe what `thread-queue-parallel` does) or remove the now-misleading sentence about parallel using multithreading.

Assert used for runtime type check in production code

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit contains `assert isinstance(message.value, BrokerValue)` as a runtime type guard. Asserts are stripped under `python -O`, which is used by some production images and packaging tools. If the assumption is ever violated (e.g., an upstream change delivers a non-BrokerValue message.value), the code will silently fall into the broad `except Exception` block, the message will be marked complete and committed without ever being processed (data loss). Use an explicit `if not isinstance(...):` check and either drop via DLQ or raise.

Docstring claims consistent group→queue assignment, but hash() is process-randomized

FixedQueuePool's docstring promises "Each group is consistently assigned to the same queue" and `get_queue_for_group` is implemented as `return hash(group_key) % self.num_queues`. CPython randomizes the string hash seed per process unless `PYTHONHASHSEED` is fixed, so two runs of the consumer can map the same group to different queues. The test `test_consistent_group_assignment` only checks within a single process, so the cross-process case is not covered. In practice ordering survives because Kafka's per-partition order pins messages to one partition and that partition's items all map to one queue within a single process — but the docstring's literal claim is false and will mislead anyone reasoning about the code. Either use a stable hash (e.g. `hashlib.blake2b(group_key, ...).digest()` mod num_queues) or correct the docstring to describe the actual guarantee.

Sentry transaction name uses 'monitors.' prefix for the uptime consumer

OrderedQueueWorker.run names its Sentry transaction `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`. This consumer is registered for `Topic.UPTIME_RESULTS` (see `sentry.consumers.KAFKA_CONSUMERS["uptime-results"]` and the UptimeResultsStrategyFactory subclass), so the prefix should be `uptime.` (or some neutral identifier). The same incorrect `monitors.` prefix is used by the existing code in `result_consumer.py:49`, which is why it likely got copy-pasted here; the new transaction should be fixed so traces and performance dashboards for this consumer are correctly grouped. ResultProcessor's transaction (result_consumer.py:49) has the same problem and was inherited by this PR through the new processing path.

Submit error path silently drops messages and commits their offsets

The broad `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit catches any failure during decoding, building the WorkItem, invoking `grouping_fn`, or calling `queue_pool.submit`. When caught, it calls `offset_tracker.add_offset(...)` followed immediately by `complete_offset(...)`. Because the offset is now present in `all_offsets` and absent from `outstanding`, the commit loop treats it as fully processed and calls `commit_function({partition: offset})`. The Kafka offset advances, the message is never queued, and the work item is permanently lost with only a `logger.exception` line as evidence. This is broader than the explicit `if result is None:` path (which mirrors existing decode-failure behavior) and will silently drop messages on any bug in user-provided code (e.g. `grouping_fn`). At minimum, the message should be routed to the DLQ, or the exception should be re-raised to crash the consumer and force investigation. Note that `uptime-results` is configured without a `dlq_topic` in `KAFKA_CONSUMERS`, so there is no DLQ to send to; this should be addressed before relying on the mode.

WorkItem.message field is written but never read

`WorkItem.message` is set by `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` when constructing the work item, but no code path ever reads it (the worker only accesses `work_item.partition`, `work_item.offset`, and `work_item.result`). Either it should be used (e.g. for DLQ routing on exception, or for re-injecting on retry) or it should be removed from the dataclass to avoid carrying a dead reference to the original Message.

test_concurrent_processing_across_groups does not actually verify concurrency

The test submits 6 items split across 3 group_keys and asserts that `groups_seen` ends up with 3 distinct groups in `processed_items`. This would pass even if all 6 items were processed sequentially in a single worker (the test only checks that all groups were visited, not that they were visited in parallel). To genuinely test concurrency, the result_processor should record the timestamps (or an overlap window) at which it starts processing each item and assert that items for different groups were processed simultaneously, or use a thread-aware assertion such as verifying that processing started for at least two different groups before any single item completed.

false_positives.candidate:
Brittle exact call-count assertion for applyTemplateVariables

The updated test 'Interpolates queries before running' asserts expect(datasource.applyTemplateVariables).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(5). That count is tied to the current number of shard groups/requests produced by splitQueriesByStreamShard (currently 4 runSplitQuery sub-requests + 1 from runShardSplitQuery). Any future refactor that changes how shard groups are partitioned or merged - including the legitimate optimization of skipping the redundant second interpolation noted above - will break this test even when behavior is otherwise correct. Asserting on the final runQuery args, or checking the spy was called at least once per non-hidden target, would be more robust.

Double interpolation of targets in sharded split path

runShardSplitQuery() now calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() on every non-hidden target, then build sub-requests via interpolateShardingSelector and passes them to runSplitQuery(). runSplitQuery() then calls datasource.applyTemplateVariables() again on the same targets (querySplitting.ts line 299). Because variables such as $__auto and $step have already been substituted on the first pass, the second pass is a no-op string scan over every expr/step for every shard sub-request. While idempotent, this is wasted work proportional to (number_of_subqueries × targets_per_subquery). Consider detecting already-interpolated queries or pushing the interpolation responsibility to a single layer so the work is done once.

applyTemplateVariables mock mutates input instead of returning a new object

The beforeEach mock for applyTemplateVariables does `query.expr = query.expr.replace(...); return query;`, i.e. it returns the SAME object reference with mutated fields. The real DataSource implementation in Grafana returns a fresh object via spread (`return { ...query, expr: ... }`), so the tests run against a fake implementation that mutates the caller's targets array. If someone fixes the mock to mirror the real implementation - or if the production code starts assuming the return is a new object - the test expectations (which look at the same query objects via runQuery mock.calls) can pass for the wrong reason. Recommend splitting the mock to return a new object so tests stay aligned with production semantics.

querySupportsSplitting check now operates on already-interpolated expr

applyTemplateVariables is called before querySupportsSplitting and partition. querySupportsSplitting() relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) returning true to keep $__range-bearing queries out of the split path (see the inline comment about backend interpolation with the split timeRange). Once $__range / $__range_s / $__range_ms have been substituted into numeric strings by applyTemplateVariables, isQueryWithRangeVariable can no longer recognise them and those queries will silently fall through into normalQueries and get split. The behavior change is benign for $__auto / $step but potentially incorrect for $__range queries, since the FRONTEND now substitutes them with the dashboard range while each sub-request still carries the chunk's range. Either guard the interpolation (skip applyTemplateVariables for queries that contain a $__range variable) or update querySupportsSplitting to detect the substituted form, and add a test covering a $__range expression.

During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.

traceID field dropped from Plugin Request Completed log line

The old LoggerMiddleware.logRequest explicitly retrieved the trace ID via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) and appended it to the log params when non-empty. The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.

false_positives.candidate:
FromContext doc comment is incorrect

The comment "FromContext returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context" implies FromContext merges additional context into the receiver, but the implementation (grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext in logger.go) actually extracts a *log.ConcreteLogger that was previously stored in ctx (via log.WithContextualAttributes) and rewraps it. The comment should describe that FromContext returns a Logger populated with the contextual attributes already present in ctx (returning a fresh logger if none are found). The same wording was previously used for New, where it is also inaccurate because New takes variadic any key/value pairs, not a context.

LoggerMiddleware silently loses fields when ContextualLoggerMiddleware is absent

If anyone reorders, removes, or conditionally skips ContextualLoggerMiddleware (the middleware is newly added and easy to miss), the "Plugin Request Completed" log line will lose endpoint, pluginId, uname, dsName, dsUID with no warning. New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test file

The PR adds a brand-new middleware (NewContextualLoggerMiddleware / ContextualLoggerMiddleware) that is now responsible for enriching the request context with endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname, and the LoggerMiddleware was changed to depend on that enrichment. Despite this, no contextual_logger_middleware_test.go is added. The existing tests only cover the renamed MetricsMiddleware. Without a test that exercises the four endpoints (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) and verifies the contextual attributes are attached to the context, regressions in the enrichment logic (e.g. wrong field names, missing nil checks, or an endpoint that forgets to call instrumentContext) will not be caught.

New doc comment misdescribes the parameter

The comment "New returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context" was left unchanged, but New takes ctx ...any (key/value pairs) — not a context.Context. Combined with the newly added FromContext that does take a context.Context, the two methods are easy to confuse.
